data.content_ref: inline:{"analogy":null,"claim":"Counterexample to the claim: a decentralized network of small services can be strictly less resilient than a single large service if the network's topology creates a centralization bottleneck (e.g., a shared DNS provider, a common CA, or a network routing hub) that the large service has internalized and diversified, making the 'decentralized' network a single point of failure in disguise.","counterconditions":[{"case":"The decentralized network uses a fully peer-to-peer discovery and routing mechanism with no central hubs.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"The large service cannot effectively internalize and diversify its routing and naming infrastructure.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"The external dependencies of the decentralized network are themselves perfectly redundant.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"}],"definitions":[],"derivation":[],"formalization_refs":[],"mechanism":"Decentralization of compute does not imply decentralization of routing, naming, or trust. If all small services rely on the same external infrastructure to discover or authenticate each other, that infrastructure becomes a correlated failure point. A large service can build internal, redundant alternatives to these external dependencies, achieving higher true independence.","premises":[],"schema":"deepreason-reasoning-envelope-v1","scope":{"covers":[],"excludes":[]},"simulation_refs":[],"uncertainties":[]}
